activities.anchor: The trajectory is strikingly uniform across languages and cultures
activities.caption: line up the acquisition timeline
activities.name: paTimelineOrder

config.prompt: The schedule is strikingly uniform — order the milestones:
items: two-word combinations, word order already correct — 18–24 months
the morphological and syntactic explosion — years 2–4
config.why: Near the first birthday, perceptual tuning: infants initially discriminate every phonetic contrast in every language, then lose the contrasts their language ignores (Werker and Tees) — the dialect-specific ear is learned.

activities.anchor: Even more telling is what children get
activities.caption: pair each telltale error with what it proves
activities.name: paErrorsMatch

config.prompt: The evidence for rules — pair each finding with what it proves:

pairs.right: plurals for nonsense words — a rule, not a memorised list

pairs.left: the U-shaped curve — "goed" after months of "went"
pairs.right: a rule colliding with stored exceptions; imitation cannot produce it

pairs.left: the question that never goes linear (Crain and Nakayama, 1987)
pairs.right: structure-dependent rules from the start — no simple induction teaches them
as diagnostic as the ones that do

config.why: Four-year-olds say "wugs" for a creature they have never seen: they must possess the rule itself — the methodological breakthrough of 1958.

activities.caption: find the line the imitation myth would love
activities.name: paImitateSpot

config.prompt: One line of this summary is the imitation myth speaking — click it:
lines: Children end up speaking like their communities, so imitation feels like the default explanation.
The U-shaped curve is decisive against it.
No adult models "goed", so a memorised copy cannot produce it.
The wug test clinches it with words the child has never heard.
config.correction: Correction speeds nothing — "goed" came from "add -ed" colliding with stored exceptions, not from anything the input contained.
config.why: A memorised copy cannot produce an error the input never contained — which is why the U-shaped curve is the decisive evidence.

activities.anchor: Chomsky's argument runs: the child's input is finite
activities.caption: run the nurture–nature trial yourself
activities.name: paPovertyBranch

config.root: The claim on trial: is the grammar machinery partly innate (universal grammar), or do general learning mechanisms suffice? You design the evidence.

start.text: Which line of evidence do you pull first?

choices.label: Test statistical learning in infants
choices.feedback: Saffran and colleagues (1996): 8-month-olds segment words from fluent speech using transitional probabilities after minutes of exposure — real and powerful.

choices.label: Test what the input cannot contain
choices.feedback: Structure-dependence, binding, islands: knowledge the input does not plausibly contain — the heart of the innateness case.

choices.label: Test constructionist abstraction
choices.feedback: Tomasello: item-specific constructions ("want X", "gonna V") abstract only gradually — and distributional statistics are richer than intuitions suggest.

stats.text: Statistical learning is real — but word segmentation is a long way from syntax.

choices.label: Push it to the hard cases
choices.feedback: Whether general mechanisms scale to all of syntax is exactly what remains open.

poverty.text: Rapid, uniform convergence on rich, specific grammar — including knowledge the input lacks — keeps the innate-machinery case alive.

choices.label: And the usage-based reply?
choices.feedback: Richer input statistics and gradual abstraction — the modern counter-case.

usage.text: The modern position is genuinely unresolved: statistical learning is real and powerful, but whether general mechanisms suffice for all of syntax — with timing, species specificity and the creole evidence still pointing the other way — is the field's open core.

config.why: Each card's strength is another's weakness — which is why the field argues with data rather than intuitions.

activities.anchor: large age-of-arrival studies in second language and late ASL learners show a smooth, monotonic decline
activities.caption: place where the window bites hardest
activities.name: paWindowPlace

config.prompt: The curves show ultimate attainment dropping smoothly with first exposure. Before what age is the fall steepest?
config.why: Steepest before roughly 7, flattening after puberty (Lenneberg proposed the window, 1967). The deprivation cases — Genie, found at 13 in 1970 — show lasting syntactic deficits; late learners can be superbly fluent and accurate: what declines is the chance of fully native-like intuitions. A window closing gradually, not a door slamming at thirteen.

activities.anchor: The bilingual brain retired the last folk myth
activities.caption: true or false — the co-active mind
activities.name: paBilingualJudge

statements.s: Both languages are co-active even in single-language use.
statements.why: Cross-language priming and interlingual homophones show it — managing them is a continuous attentional task.

statements.s: Switching carries measurable costs — milliseconds in switch trials.
statements.why: Yet fluent code-switching is grammatically disciplined, not random.

statements.s: The claimed executive-function advantage (Bialystok) has replicated cleanly at scale.
statements.why: Paap's failed replications and publication-bias analyses cut the effect down — the honest summary: far-reaching benefits unproven, co-activation certain.

statements.s: Bilingual children meet milestones on schedule, sometimes with vocabulary distributed across the two languages.
statements.why: The last folk myth — that two languages confuse a child — is retired.

activities.caption: fill the two milestones of the bilingual and literate mind
activities.name: paChildCloze

config.text: Children raised with two languages from birth differentiate them early (by roughly age %%2%%, adjusting language choice to interlocutor), meet milestones on schedule with vocabulary distributed across the two lexicons, and mix mid-sentence only where both grammars allow. Reading, meanwhile, must be taught: it rides on %%phonological awareness%% — the discovery that speech decomposes into phonemes, which letters represent.
config.hint: A single digit; and the best-established predictor-intervention in education.

activities.anchor: Comprehension gets the headlines, but production is where the architecture shows its seams
activities.caption: assemble Levelt's pipeline
activities.name: paLeveltOrder

config.prompt: From thought to sound — order the stages:
items: the conceptualiser turns intention into a preverbal message
the formulator retrieves lemmas and builds phonological form
the monitor listens to your own speech for errors
config.why: The evidence is the error pattern: tip-of-the-tongue splits lemma from phonology (meaning known, sound missing); "you have hissed my mystery lectures" strands s across words — planning chunks larger than the word. Production is rule-governed machinery, and its slips are the machine's blueprints; second-language fluency is precisely this pipeline's automatization.
